checks.claim: Key: rocks, seawater, air and every part of the body are built from atoms; atoms are the building blocks of all ordinary matter
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Atoms form the basis of all ordinary matter in the universe.' Wikipedia agrees ('fundamental building blocks of matter'). The dissolved salt in seawater is present as ions, which are charged atoms (Wikipedia: 'A charged atom is called an ion'), so the key still holds.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Cells': cells are the unit of living things only, so rocks, seawater and air are not built of cells
checks.note: 'the fundamental structural, functional, and biological unit of all known living organisms'. Cannot cover rocks or air, so wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Crystals': rocks are mostly mineral crystals, but seawater and air are not made of crystals
checks.note: Minerals have 'an ordered atomic arrangement, often manifesting as single crystals'. Air and seawater are not crystalline, so the choice fails for most of the list. Wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Germs': germs are microscopic organisms (bacteria, fungi, protozoa, viruses) that can cause disease; rocks, water and air are not built of them
checks.note: Wrong. Minor nuance in the context's 'germs are tiny living things': viruses are counted as germs and whether they are alive is debated. Acceptable child-level wording; optionally 'germs are tiny living things that can make us ill' stays safe since most germs are.

checks.claim: Context: cells, germs and the crystals in a rock are all made of atoms
checks.note: Crystals are ordered arrangements of atoms; cells are made of water, proteins, lipids and other molecules (Grokipedia Cell), which are made of atoms.

checks.claim: Key: the pumped-up ball weighs a little more because air has weight (and the gain is real and measurable)
checks.note: Prof. Louis Bloomfield (How Everything Works): the air in a properly inflated basketball weighs about 0.03 lb, but buoyancy from the surrounding air supports about 0.02 lb, so the ball holds 'about 0.01 pounds of extra air' that registers on a scale, roughly 4-5 g. My own check agrees: a size-7 ball holds about 7 L; at about 8 psi gauge the extra air is about 0.55 x 1.2 g/L x 7 L, about 4.6 g. A basketball weighs about 600 g, so a kitchen or school gram balance shows the gain. Classroom lessons run exactly this (howtosmile.org/node/2476: 'The inflated ball has the greater mass'), and NGSS 5-PS1-1 names 'adding air to expand a basketball' as evidence.

checks.claim: Air has mass (density of dry air about 1.2 kg per cubic metre)
checks.note: 1.225 kg/m3 at sea level, 15 C.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'A little less, because air makes things lighter'
checks.note: Wrong: buoyancy only cancels the share of the air that is at outside pressure; the extra squeezed-in air still adds weight, so the reading rises, never falls.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'The same, because air has no weight'
checks.note: Wrong: air has mass. (A ball filled only to outside pressure would read the same because of buoyancy, but 'pumps it full' means pressurised, and the stated reason, 'air has no weight', is false in any case.)

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'A little more, because its skin is stretched tight'; context: stretching adds nothing to its weight
checks.note: Stretching changes no amount of matter in the skin; the gain comes only from the added air. Wrong as intended.

checks.claim: Key: only the sealed syringe holding air lets the plunger be pushed in
checks.note: Gases have 'high compressibility due to the large average distance between particles'; Grokipedia notes gases are roughly 20,000 times more compressible than liquids. NGSS 5-PS1-1 names 'compressing air in a syringe' as evidence.

checks.claim: Water hardly compresses at all (context: 'hardly squeezes at all and its plunger stays put')
checks.note: Water's bulk modulus is about 2.2 GPa. A hand pushing on a syringe gives well under 1 MPa, a volume change of a few hundredths of a percent, far too small to see. The context's 'hardly' is properly hedged.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Only the one holding water'
checks.note: Reversed; wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Both, by the same amount'
checks.note: Wrong: air compresses about 20,000 times more readily than water.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Neither, even a little'
checks.note: Wrong: the air plunger moves in noticeably.

checks.claim: Context: there is empty space between a gas's particles; water's particles are packed close together
checks.note: Gas particles 'widely separated'; 'liquid molecules are already in close contact'. Matches the NGSS grade 5 particle model.

checks.claim: Key: tiny particles that come off the roses travel to her nose
checks.note: Odor arises from 'volatile chemical compounds'; 'volatile odorant molecules enter the nasal cavity via inhalation'.

checks.claim: The scent's particles leave the petals (context)
checks.note: Floral scent is VOCs 'emitted primarily from floral tissues such as petals', allowing 'detection over distances'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Air particles the roses have made smelly'; context: the air itself does not turn smelly
checks.note: Wrong: the odorants are the rose's own molecules mixed among the air's; air molecules do not take on a smell. A known misconception ('reacts with the air', York BEST probe).

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'A wave that spreads the way sound does'
checks.note: Wrong: smell is carried by airborne molecules, not a wave. (The fringe vibration theory of smell concerns how receptors read a molecule, not how a smell travels, so it does not rescue this choice.)

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Nothing, since a smell is not matter'
checks.note: Wrong: odorants are matter (molecules).

checks.claim: Context: the particles drift through the air, too small to see
checks.note: Diffusion of perfume vapour through still air is Grokipedia's own example; air currents also carry it. 'Drift' covers both.

checks.claim: Key: dissolved salt has broken up into particles and spread through the water
checks.note: 'The dissolution of sodium chloride in water involves the separation of Na+ and Cl- ions from the ionic lattice'; Grokipedia Solution: particles 'uniformly dispersed at the molecular or ionic level', 'no distinct particles ... can be observed'.

checks.claim: A spoonful dissolves fully in a beaker and the water stays clear
checks.note: Solubility 360 g per kg of water at 25 C, so a spoonful (about 6-18 g) dissolves fully in any beaker. Salt water is clear. (Table salt with anti-caking agents can leave faint cloudiness, too minor to matter.)

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'It has melted, the way ice melts'; context: salt melts only at about 800 degrees Celsius
checks.note: Melting point 800.7 C; 'about 800' is right. Dissolving is not melting. Wrong as intended.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'It has turned into water'
checks.note: Wrong: the salt's ions stay sodium and chloride, dispersed in the water.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'It has vanished from the water for good'; context: the water tastes of it and the salt comes back when the water dries up
checks.note: Wrong: evaporating the water returns the salt as crystals (Grokipedia Salt evaporation pond: sunlight and wind 'remove water to concentrate and crystallize the dissolved minerals'; University of Hawaii activity https://manoa.hawaii.edu/exploringourfluidearth/chemical/chemistry-and-seawater/salty-sea/activity-recovering-salts-seawater has students weigh the 'dry crystals' left after evaporation). 'The water tastes of it' is likewise true of salt water.

checks.claim: Key: when the seawater dries up, the salt is left in the dish as white crystals
checks.note: Evaporation 'removes freshwater vapor and concentrates salts'; seawater holds about 35 g of salts per kg, about 85 percent sodium and chloride. Grokipedia Halite: 'colorless or white' crystals that form 'through the evaporation of saline water bodies'. A dish of 3.5 percent brine leaves a visible white crust.

checks.claim: Clear seawater holds dissolved salt too small to see (context)
checks.note: Salt water is a true solution; no particles can be seen.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'It rose into the air along with the water'
checks.note: Wrong: only water vapour leaves; salt does not evaporate at room temperature (it boils near 1,465 C). Sea spray can put salt into the air at the ocean, but by bursting bubbles and waves, not by a still dish drying.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'It soaked into the glass of the dish'
checks.note: Wrong: glass is not porous; the crystals sit on its surface. (Matches misconception M5.)

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'It was used up by the heat of the Sun'
checks.note: Wrong: sunlight only drives off the water; the salt remains.

checks.claim: Context: salt-makers dry seawater in shallow ponds in the same way
checks.note: 'sunlight and wind gradually remove water to concentrate and crystallize the dissolved minerals'; NaCl crystals 'settle on the pond floor'.

checks.claim: Key: steel is made of particles far too small to see
checks.note: Atoms are 'typically around 100 picometers across' and 'cannot be viewed using an optical microscope'. NGSS PS1.A grade 5: 'Matter of any type can be subdivided into particles that are too small to see'.

checks.claim: Context: not even the strongest school microscope can show them
checks.note: Optical resolution is 'fundamentally limited to about 200-250 nanometers', 'preventing atomic-scale imaging'; atoms are about 0.1-0.5 nm (Grokipedia Atom), roughly a thousand times smaller. School microscopes are optical; only special instruments (scanning tunnelling microscope) map atoms.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'One solid piece with no parts'
checks.note: Wrong: matter 'is composed of atoms' (continuous-matter misconception M6).

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Particles with air in the gaps'; context: no air fills the tiny gaps
checks.note: Wrong: the grade 5 model has 'empty space between those particles'; RSC (https://edu.rsc.org/resources/students-ideas-about-the-particulate-nature-of-matter-beyond-appearances/4017763.article) lists air, dust or other gases in the gaps as a known misconception. Air is itself made of particles and cannot sit between a metal's atoms.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Particles a magnifying glass can show'
checks.note: Wrong: if a full optical microscope cannot show atoms, a magnifying glass cannot. (Steel's crystal grains, micrometres wide, show only under a microscope after polishing and etching, and they are not 'the particles' of the particle model, so they do not make this choice defensible.)

checks.claim: Stem: matter is anything that has mass and takes up space
checks.note: 'any substance that has mass and occupies space'; the Amplify grade 5 lesson uses the same definition.

checks.claim: Key: a beam of sunlight is not matter; sunlight has no mass
checks.note: The photon is 'a massless, chargeless elementary particle' with 'zero rest mass'. Grokipedia Matter contrasts matter with energy, and says photons 'do not contribute to the material substance of matter'. The grade 5 curriculum says 'Light, heat, and sound are not matter because they don't have mass or take up space' (Amplify, via pengi.ai). Under the stem's own definition the key is correct. (Photons carry energy and momentum, and some writers speak of light's 'relativistic mass', but no standard definition counts light as matter.)

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'A breath of air' is matter
checks.note: Grokipedia lists 'the air in a room (gas)' as matter; air has a density of about 1.2 kg/m3.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'A cloud of steam' is matter
checks.note: 'Steam is the gaseous phase of water'; the visible white cloud is 'aerosols of microscopic liquid water droplets'. Matter either way.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'A puff of smoke' is matter
checks.note: 'a visible aerosol consisting of solid particles, liquid droplets, and gases'. Matter. None of the three wrong choices is not matter, so the question has one answer.

checks.claim: Context: light, like heat and sound, is a form of energy
checks.note: Standard school wording (NASA Chandra handout describes light as energy; NGSS 4-PS3-2 has energy carried by sound, light and heat). Physicists would say light carries energy rather than being 'pure energy' (C. Baird, West Texas A&M: 'Light is not pure energy'), but 'a form of energy' is the accepted child-level phrase and is not false. Optional safer wording: 'light, like heat and sound, carries energy but is not matter.' Note also that the beam seen slanting through a room shows because of dust it lights up; the light itself is still not matter.

unit_notes: All 8 questions check out. Key points looked at hard: (1) Basketball: the gain is real and measurable. Buoyancy cancels the air at outside pressure, but the extra pumped-in air, about 0.01 lb (roughly 4-5 g, per Prof. Louis Bloomfield, How Everything Works), registers on a gram scale against a ball of about 600 g. (2) Sunlight: not matter by the stem's own definition (massless photon); air, steam and smoke are all matter, so there is one answer. (3) Minor optional wording notes only: 'germs are tiny living things' (viruses are germs of debated life status) and 'light is a form of energy' (physicists prefer 'carries energy'); neither is an error at grade 5.
